title: Redis Data Types
description: Explore Redis core data structures: Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, and Sorted Sets with practical C# and Node.js examples.

data.text: Redis is often called a data structure server because it does not just store raw values — it stores rich data types and lets you manipulate them atomically. Understanding these five core types is the foundation of every Redis-backed application.

Strings are the simplest Redis type. They can hold text or binary data up to 512 MB and support operations like `GET`, `SET`, `INCR`, and `EXPIRE`. Strings are ideal for caching HTML fragments, JSON payloads, counters, and feature flags.

data.content: Use StackExchange.Redis to store and retrieve a JSON string.

data.text: Hashes store field-value pairs under a single key. They are perfect for representing objects such as user profiles or product details. You can read or update individual fields without fetching the entire value.

data.title: When to use each type
items: **List** — ordered sequences with duplicates. Use for job queues, recent activity feeds, or chat history.
**Set** — unordered unique values. Use for tags, followers, or visit tracking.
**Sorted Set** — unique values ranked by a numeric score. Use for leaderboards, rate-limited queues, and time-series indexes.

terms.definition: An operation that completes fully or not at all. Redis commands are atomic by default, so concurrent clients never see partial state.
Redis internally re-encodes values for memory efficiency. For example, small hashes can be stored as a single compact object.

data.title: Choosing the right type
data.text: If you only need one field, a String is simpler and faster than a Hash. Use Hashes when you need to update individual fields without rewriting the whole object.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Redis Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, and Sorted Sets cover most application data-modeling needs.
Pick the type that matches your access pattern to keep operations fast and memory-efficient.
All Redis commands are atomic, so you get safe concurrency without extra locking code.
